name: Lamba
catalog_quote: The stress in Lamba is normally on the penultimate syllable of each word, and in this way is to a great extent the determining factor in word-division.… Unlike Zulu the penultimate stress is not of necessity accompanied by length. Penultimate length is merely incidental in Lamba.
sweep_summary: One title-keyword item for Lamba: Bickmore 1995 'Tone and stress in Lamba' (Phonology 12(3):307-341), squarely about word stress/accent in this language and the only modern fieldwork-based study of it. No open copy exists (OpenAlex closed, no OA URL at Crossref/S2/OpenAIRE/BASE/scholar.archive.org, author's old Albany site now behind SSO with no Wayback snapshot); only the Cambridge first-page preview (p.307, introduction) and Extract were readable and saved with scanned under That page frames Lamba as a hybrid metrical+tonal prominence system but is silent on placement. The author's 2024 CV (fetched sources) confirms the citation and Lamba fieldwork in Zambia. Priority high for acquisition (Harvard online via HOLLIS; DOI 10.1017/S0952675700002542): the held secondary summary (de Lacy 2002 fn.10) says Bickmore's data disagree with Doke's audible penult stress, so the full text could downgrade the catalog's fixed-strict coding; that claim remains unverified first-hand. The best first-hand statement read in this sweep is Doke 1922:10 (already on file): penultimate main stress with alternating secondary stress and a few antepenult exceptions -- confirms/refines, does not supersede, the catalog's Doke 1938:33 quote. updated.

new_statements.quote: The general Bantu rule is that the stress of a word falls on the penultimate syllable ; e.g., awantu (people), pendulala (count over), iffnji (many), paéma (beat). [...] There are, however, a few exceptions, which retain the stress on the antepenultimate syllable. Cf. umwanice (youngster), umtsice (unmarried person) [...] Cf. also the perfect stems of fit-, nunk- and Wip-, when used adjectivally [...] In polysyllabic words, while the main stress rests on the penultimate syllable, there is a secondary stress on alternate syllables.
new_statements.citation: Doke, Clement M. 1922. The Grammar of the Lamba Language. London: Kegan Paul, Trench, Trubner. p.10, sec. 6(C)(i)(a) 'Word Stress' (Google Books id pJ5kAAAAMAAJ, US full view; page image + tesseract scanned fetched sources in the 2026-09-16 pass, re-read now)
new_statements.locator: p.10, (C) Stress, (i) Normal Stress, (a) Word Stress
new_statements.reading: Main word stress on the penultimate syllable, secondary stress on alternate syllables leftward, a handful of lexical/morphological antepenult exceptions (diminutive -ice nouns, adjectival perfect stems), and monosyllabic stems throwing stress onto the preceding particle (still penult of the group). Supports the catalog's fixed-penult coding; the exceptions and the alternating secondary stress are refinements (srule + caution), not a recode. scanned accents are partly garbled (awantu = aŵántu, pendulala = pendulúla, iffnji = ifínji, paéma = páma); the accent placement was verified against the page image in the earlier pass.

audit.recode_to: Undetermined until Bickmore 1995 is read. If Bickmore denies audible penultimate stress (as de Lacy 2002 fn.10 implies) the record cannot stay 'fixed-strict penult' on Doke alone: candidates are a caution/contra entry (Doke 1922/1938 penult vs Bickmore 1995 left-edge trochaic metrical structure in the prefix domain, tone-diagnosed) or a recode to a morphology-anchored/left-edge rhythmic class. Independently, Doke 1922:10 supports adding srule = secondary stress on alternate syllables counting back from the penult, and noting a few lexical antepenult exceptions (umwánice, -fítile), which bears on 'strict'.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote: confirmed verbatim in the held Hyman 2013 text (kuan1247/ l.89-92), which is exactly the locus the record cites; primary Doke 1938 not held. (2) Deciding source: a 1938 reference grammar read second-hand via a 2013 article; impressionistic. A dedicated fieldwork-based Phonology article on Lamba tone AND stress (Bickmore 1995) exists, is not held, is closed access, and a held paper (de Lacy 2002:15 fn.10) explicitly records that it disagrees with Doke's audible penult stress. That is the definition of at-risk: a better source plausibly changes the coding. (3) fetched sources now: Doke 1922 pp.1-20 (open, saved with scanned; p.10 confirms penult main stress but adds secondary stress on alternate syllables and a few antepenult exceptions (refines rule/srule/strict). Mwape 2012 (held) is silent on

sources.quote: p.10: 'The general Bantu rule is that the stress of a word falls on the penultimate syllable; e.g., awântu (people), pendulúla (count over), ifínji (many), páma (beat). ... There are, however, a few exceptions, which retain the stress on the antepenultimate syllable. Cf. umwánice (youngster), umúsice (unmarried person) ... Cf. also the perfect stems ... -fítile (black), -núŋkile (smelling), and -ŵípile (evil). Further, certain verb simple stems, being monosyllabic, and monosyllabic noun stems ... throw back the stress on to the particle preceding ... e.g., ukú lya (to eat), wá ya (he has gone)
sources.note: Open first-hand Doke statement (fetched sources now): penult main stress, secondary stress on alternate syllables, a few antepenult lexical exceptions -- usable as the held primary locus instead of a second-hand 1938 excerpt.

sources.quote: It has long been observed that not all languages fit neatly into a 'stress' vs. 'tone' dichotomy. Recent research has concentrated on how to account formally for 'hybrid' prominence systems which have been argued to exhibit both metrical and tonal properties. Generally this entails postulating both a tonal and metrical (or accentual) tier.

sources.note: The only modern, fieldwork-based study of Lamba stress; held de Lacy 2002 fn.10 says it disagrees with Doke 1938's audible penultimate stress and instead describes left-edge trochaic footing of a pre-root domain diagnosed by H-tone placement -- our fixed-strict-penult coding rests solely on the Doke sentence it disputes.
